## Applied Exercises

As in the earlier chapters, work on these exercises in a fresh copy of your analysis workbook, made after you finish this chapter's tutorials. Put each exercise on its own worksheets, named after it, and do not rename or edit the queries the tutorials created. When an exercise needs a Table the tutorials filtered, import it again as a new query with the name the exercise gives.

### Financial Accounting Exercises

**Exercise 7.1: Forecasting Revenue by Product Line**

**Table group:** Order-to-Cash, with the Item table from Master Data

**Scenario.** Charles River's loan agreement requires management to send the bank, with the annual financial statements, a revenue forecast for the coming quarter by product line, which the bank uses to monitor the company's covenants. Because the forecast goes to an external user who will rely on it, the controller asks you to test the forecasting methods of Tutorial 7.1 on each product line before choosing one.

**Requirements.**

(1) Build a table of quarterly revenue by item group for 2024 through 2026 from InvoiceLines, with a quarter index from 1 to 12.

(2) For each item group, fit three methods to the eight quarters of 2024 and 2025 and forecast the four quarters of 2026: a trend with FORECAST.LINEAR, the mean, and the same quarter of the previous year. Calculate the mean absolute percentage error of each method over the four quarters.

(3) Choose a method for each item group, and explain the choice in one or two sentences per group. Consider whether the first quarter of 2024, which contains the start-up month, should be left out of the fit.

(4) Forecast the first quarter of 2027 for each item group with your chosen method, give a range for each, and compare the sum of the item-group forecasts with the company-level forecast from Tutorial 7.1.

**Deliverable.** A backtest table by item group, the chosen methods with reasons, and a forecast of the first quarter of 2027 by item group with ranges.

**Exercise 7.2: Reconciling the Budget to Its Detail**

**Table group:** Organizational Planning, with the Account table from Accounting Core

**Scenario.** The bank also receives Charles River's annual budget, and last year's budget summary for the bank was prepared from the Budget Table, which summarizes the budget by cost center and account. Before the 2027 budget is sent in the same form, the controller asks you to confirm that the summary agrees with the detailed budget lines.

**Requirements.**

(1) Import the T76_Budget Table with Power Query as a query named `BudgetSummary`. Use **Transform > Group By**, with **Advanced**, to total BudgetAmount by FiscalYear and AccountID, and merge in AccountNumber and AccountName from the Account query of Tutorial 7.2, without the prefix.

(2) Import the T77_BudgetLine Table again as a new query named `BudgetLineAll`, because the BudgetLine query of Tutorial 7.2 holds only 2026. Keep the Revenue, COGS, and Operating Expense categories of every year, and total BudgetAmount by FiscalYear and AccountID with Group By.

(3) Compare the two for 2026 by account, and list every account whose totals differ. Examine the BudgetLine rows behind the differences and identify what they have in common.

(4) Repeat the comparison for 2024 and 2025.

(5) Write a memo of half a page that explains the difference, states which Table should be used for the budget sent to the bank, and recommends a control that would detect the problem in future.

**Deliverable.** A reconciliation by account for 2026, the totals for 2024 and 2025, and a half-page memo.

### Managerial Accounting Exercises

**Exercise 7.3: Company Break-Even and Margin of Safety**

**Table group:** Order-to-Cash, Accounting Core, and Organizational Planning

**Scenario.** As part of the 2027 plan, the chief financial officer asks how far revenue could fall before Charles River stopped earning an operating profit, using 2026 as the base.

**Requirements.**

(1) Calculate the 2026 contribution margin ratio as revenue minus the standard cost of the products sold and minus the sales commission expense, divided by revenue. Use InvoiceLines for revenue and standard cost, and the GLOpex query from Tutorial 7.2 for commissions.

(2) Use the 2026 operating-expense budget, excluding sales commissions, as the fixed costs. Explain in two sentences why the budget is a reasonable source for them.

(3) Calculate the break-even revenue and the margin of safety in dollars and as a percentage of 2026 revenue.

(4) The fixed costs in (2) leave out the freight-out expense and the purchase price and manufacturing variances recorded in 2026, which GLOpex does not contain. Import the T3_GLEntry Table again as a new query named `GLCostVariances`, clicking **Transform Data**, and filter FiscalYear to 2026, AccountID to 54, 55, and 93 (accounts 5050, 5060, and 5080), and SourceDocumentType to exclude JournalEntry, whose only rows on these accounts are the closing entry. Add the three accounts' totals to the fixed costs, and recalculate the break-even revenue and margin of safety.

(5) Build a two-variable data table of break-even revenue for contribution margin ratios from 40 to 50 percent and fixed costs from $6 million to $10 million, and use Goal Seek to find the revenue that produces an operating income of $4 million under the assumptions of (4).

(6) Write a memo of half a page that states your break-even estimate and the assumption that affects it most.

**Deliverable.** A break-even model with two sets of fixed costs, a sensitivity table, and a half-page memo.

**Exercise 7.4: The Product Mix under a Capacity Constraint**

**Table group:** Manufacturing and Order-to-Cash, with the Item table from Master Data

**Scenario.** This exercise uses a hypothetical situation. Suppose that an equipment upgrade in 2027 halves the hours available in every work center for a year, while demand for each manufactured item stays at its 2026 level. In 2026, Charles River's plant used well under its capacity, so the constraint in this exercise is an assumption, not a description of the data. The operations manager asks which items to make.

**Requirements.**

(1) Import the T44_Item Table again as a new query named `ItemRouting`, keeping ItemID, ItemCode, ItemGroup, StandardCost, StandardFixedOverheadCost, SupplyMode, and RoutingID, because the Item query of Chapter 4 does not have the last three columns. Import the T50_RoutingOperation, T47_WorkCenter, and T48_WorkCenterCalendar Tables, and list the manufactured items that sold in 2026.

(2) For each item, calculate its 2026 demand in units, its contribution per unit as the 2026 average price per unit minus the variable standard cost (StandardCost minus StandardFixedOverheadCost) minus the commission rate from Tutorial 7.3 times the price, and its run hours per unit at each work center, summing StandardRunHoursPerUnit over the operations of its routing.

(3) Calculate each work center's capacity as half of its 2026 available hours, and set up the production quantities as the variable cells, the total contribution as the objective, and the hours used at each work center as SUMPRODUCT formulas. SUMPRODUCT multiplies two ranges of the same size cell by cell and adds the products, so `=SUMPRODUCT(Hours,Quantities)` gives the hours that a production plan uses.

(4) Use Solver with the Simplex LP method to maximize the total contribution, subject to hours used within capacity at every work center and production between zero and demand for every item. Do not require whole units, so that Solver can produce its Sensitivity report.

(5) Using the answer and the Sensitivity report, identify the work centers whose capacity binds, the shadow price of their hours, the items Solver reduces, and the contribution lost compared with meeting all demand.

**Deliverable.** A Solver model, its Answer and Sensitivity reports, and a half-page recommendation to the operations manager.

### Auditing Exercises

**Exercise 7.5: Regression-Based Expectations for Revenue and Commissions**

**Table group:** Order-to-Cash and Accounting Core

**Scenario.** Chapter 1 described a regression-based expectation for monthly revenue as a substantive analytical procedure. Your audit senior asks you to test whether such an expectation would be precise enough for Charles River, and to compare it with an expectation for sales commission expense. The standard on substantive analytical procedures of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) asks for expectations precise enough to identify potential material misstatements, and it notes that expectations built on monthly amounts are generally more effective than those built on annual amounts (PCAOB, n.d.-a).

**Requirements.**

(1) Build a monthly table for 2024 through 2026 with revenue from InvoiceLines and the number of invoices from the SalesInvoice Table. GLOpex holds only 2026, so import the T3_GLEntry Table again as a new query named `GLCommission`, clicking **Transform Data**, and filter AccountID to 104 (account 6290, Sales Commission Expense) and SourceDocumentType to exclude JournalEntry, whose only rows on this account are the three year-end closing entries. Add the monthly commission expense to the table.

(2) Regress monthly revenue on the number of invoices, with and without January 2024, and compare R Square and the standard error with the average monthly revenue. Explain whether the expectation would be precise enough to detect a misstatement of 5 percent of a month's revenue.

(3) Regress monthly commission expense on monthly revenue for 2024 and 2025, and use the fitted line to set an expectation for each month of 2026.

(4) Flag the 2026 months whose recorded commission expense differs from the expectation by more than 3 percent, and describe the evidence you would examine for each. Look at the signs of the differences in consecutive months.

(5) Import the T27_SalesCommissionAccrual Table, total the CommissionAmount of the accruals dated in 2026, and reconcile the total to the 2026 commission expense in GLCommission. Identify the source document type that explains the difference.

**Deliverable.** Two regressions, a table of 2026 expectations and differences, and a half-page memo to your senior.

**Exercise 7.6: Evaluating Management's Forecast**

**Table group:** Demand Planning and MRP, Order-to-Cash, and Organizational Planning

**Scenario.** Charles River's demand forecast drives its purchasing and production plans and the quantities in its budget, and management may use it to support accounting estimates, such as the need for an inventory reserve. When a company's estimates rest on assumptions, the PCAOB's standard on auditing accounting estimates asks the auditor to evaluate whether the significant assumptions are consistent with, among other things, the company's historical or recent experience (PCAOB, n.d.-b). Your senior asks you to evaluate the forecast against that experience.

**Requirements.**

(1) Import the T78_DemandForecast Table with Power Query, keeping the rows whose IsCurrent is 1, the current version. Merge in ItemGroup from the Item query without the prefix, and total ForecastQuantity by item group and by the year of ForecastWeekStartDate.

(2) Import the T10_SalesOrderLine Table as a query named `OrderLines`. Merge in OrderDate from the SalesOrder query of Tutorial 5.2 and ItemGroup from the Item query, both without the prefix, total Quantity by item group and by the year of OrderDate, and calculate the ratio of forecast to orders for each year and item group.

(3) Describe how the ratio has changed over the three years, and whether it differs among the item groups.

(4) Compare the 2026 budget's quantities with the 2026 forecast and with the 2026 orders.

(5) Each forecast records the baseline quantity that the forecasting method produced, the quantity after any planner adjustment, the planner, and the employee who approved it. Add a column with the ratio of ForecastQuantity to BaselineForecastQuantity, list the forecasts adjusted by more than half of their baseline, and look up their planners and approvers in the Employee Table. Explain which control the list tests and what it shows.

(6) Write a memo of half a page that states whether the forecast is consistent with historical experience, the consequences for any estimate or plan that relies on it, what the adjusted forecasts show about the review of planners' changes, and the evidence and explanations you would request from management.

**Deliverable.** A comparison of forecast and actual orders by year and item group, a list of the adjusted forecasts, and a half-page memo.
